course: Your first season as a coach

modules.title: Before your first session
modules.summary: Walk on to the pitch with a plan
modules.outcome: You can walk on to the pitch knowing what happens in each of the 60 minutes, and why.

why.text: Across 70 sessions by 25 youth soccer coaches, about two-thirds of the time went on drills and fitness, and a third on game-like play.
Your federation’s curriculum builds every session for this age around games.

modules.leave_with: A session you can read in one minute, a set-up you do once, and a plan B.
own_team_tiles: Minutes from arrival to first game

lessons.title: What a good session looks like at this age
lessons.one_line: Busy, lots of touches, ends with a game
lessons.idea: A good session is one where every child is moving with a ball for most of the hour. Games do that. Queues do not.
steps: Start with a game as they arrive.
Play two short games on one idea.
Finish with a real game.
words_to_use: Grab a ball and join in.
Same game, one new rule.
Last game. Go and play.
lessons.instead_of: Laps. Lines. Long talks.
lessons.try_task: Look up and count how many players are standing still. Do it at 5:10, 5:30 and 5:50.

answers.then: Carry on in order
“Keeping everyone busy” moves up to next week
“Keeping everyone busy” next, with your own session picked apart

lessons.film_brief: Three 20-second looks at one real under-11 session: the arrival game, the middle, the final game. Wide shot. A counter on screen shows how many players are moving.

lessons.title: How to read your session in Clean Sheet
lessons.one_line: The why, the set-up, what to say
lessons.idea: Each part of your session has a reason, a picture and a few words to say. Read them in that order and you are ready.
steps: Read the “Why” for each part.
Look at the set-up picture and the kit list.
Pick one thing to say and one thing to look for.
lessons.try_task: Open Tuesday’s run sheet and say the “Why” for each part out loud, in one sentence each.

answers.then: Carry on in order
That drill’s full explanation opens
A reminder two hours before training

lessons.film_brief: A screen recording of one real proposed session with a coach’s voice reading it as they would in the car park. No presenter on camera.

lessons.title: Setting up before the players arrive
lessons.one_line: Cones once, not four times
lessons.idea: If you lay out the biggest area first and build the smaller ones inside it, you set up once and never stop the session to move cones.
steps: Arrive ten minutes early.
Mark the game pitch first, then the squares inside it.
Balls and bibs in one pile by the gate.
words_to_use: Balls are by the gate. Grab one.
lessons.instead_of: Setting up each game while they wait.
lessons.try_task: Lay out the final game pitch and both squares before 5:00. Don’t move a cone until the game.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A one-page set-up picture is added to your run sheets
Your sessions are proposed with a simpler set-up for three weeks

lessons.film_brief: Overhead or high-angle time-lapse of a coach laying out one pitch with two squares inside it, in under four minutes. Captions name each step.

lessons.title: Your first two minutes
lessons.one_line: Names, one signal, straight into a game
lessons.idea: Children decide in the first two minutes whether tonight is fun. Greet them by name, give one signal, and get them playing.
steps: Say hello to each player by name at the gate.
Teach one signal: hand up means ball under your foot.
First game running inside two minutes.
words_to_use: Hi Ari. Grab a ball.
When my hand goes up, ball under your foot.
Off you go.
lessons.instead_of: Waiting for everyone before you start.
lessons.try_task: Use the hand-up signal three times in the arrival game. Wait until every ball is still before you speak.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A tip is added to next week’s run sheet
“Getting their attention without shouting” moves up to next week

lessons.film_brief: A real coach at the gate greeting players by name, then the hand-up signal working. Shot from behind the coach so we see the players’ response.

lessons.title: When it is not working
lessons.one_line: Make it easier, make it harder, or move on
lessons.idea: Every game can be changed in three ways: the space, the numbers or one rule. If a change doesn’t fix it, move on. That is not failing.
steps: Watch for two minutes before you change anything.
Change one thing: space, numbers or a rule.
Still not working? Go to the next game.
words_to_use: Same game, bigger square.
Now you only get two touches.
Good effort. Next game.
lessons.instead_of: Stopping to explain it again, slower.
lessons.try_task: Use the “too hard” or “too easy” line from your run sheet on one game, even if it is going fine.

answers.answer: Made it easier and it worked
answers.then: Carry on in order

answers.answer: Made it harder and it worked
answers.then: Carry on in order
That drill is swapped out of your suggestions for a month
We ask again next week

lessons.film_brief: One keep-ball game failing, then the same game with a bigger square working. Split screen before and after, 15 seconds each.

modules.title: Keeping players safe
modules.summary: Head knocks, heat, injuries, who to tell
modules.outcome: You know what to do, and who to tell, when a child is hurt or something worries you.

why.text: Australian guidelines say a child with a suspected concussion sits out, and does not play a game for at least 21 days.
Your club asks every new coach to finish this module by round 3.

modules.leave_with: The head-knock rule, your club’s heat rule, and the name and number of your welfare officer, saved to your phone.

lessons.title: Head knocks: if in doubt, sit them out
lessons.one_line: Off straight away, and no game for at least 21 days
lessons.idea: You don’t have to decide whether it is a concussion. If a player takes a knock to the head and anything seems off, they stop for the day and a doctor decides.
steps: Take them off straight away. They don’t go back on today.
Tell the parent and log it in the app.
They need 14 days with no symptoms before contact training, and at least 21 days before a game.
words_to_use: You’re sitting out now. That’s my call, not yours.
It may be nothing. The rule is that a doctor checks first.
lessons.instead_of: “Shake it off.” “See how you feel in five minutes.”
lessons.try_task: Find “Log a head knock” on your phone and find out who your club’s first-aider is.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A message to your club is drafted for you
A reminder before Sunday’s game

lessons.film_brief: A club first-aider and a coach walking through a staged sideline moment with an adult standing in for the player. Calm tone. The three steps on screen.

lessons.title: Heat, storms and bad air
lessons.one_line: Check before you leave home
lessons.idea: Heat risk depends on temperature and humidity together. Sports Medicine Australia publishes a tool for it and your federation sets the rule. Your job is to check and follow it.
steps: Check the heat rating for your ground before you leave.
Do what it says: more breaks and shade, a shorter session, or stop.
Thunder or lightning: everyone off, and follow your federation’s rule to restart.
words_to_use: Drinks break. Everyone, now.
We’re finishing early today. It’s too hot to be fair on you.
lessons.instead_of: Pushing on because parents drove a long way.
lessons.try_task: Open your club’s heat rule from the Home screen and add a drinks break to Tuesday’s run sheet.

answers.then: Carry on in order
Your director is told a coach couldn’t find it, without your name
A reminder on the next day over 30 degrees

lessons.film_brief: A sports doctor or club official explaining the heat tool in plain words over footage of a shaded drinks break. Under two minutes.

lessons.title: Injuries: what you do and what you don’t
lessons.one_line: Stop, stay calm, get help, write it down
lessons.idea: You are not the medic. Your job is to stop the game, keep the player still and calm, get the right person, and record what happened.
steps: Stop play and go to the player.
Neck or back pain, or they can’t get up: don’t move them. Call 000.
For knocks and cuts: first-aid kit, tell the parent, log it.
words_to_use: Stay still. I’m here.
Everyone else, ball under your foot and wait with Sam.
lessons.instead_of: Carrying a player off. Guessing what the injury is.
lessons.try_task: Check there is a first-aid kit in your bag and that you can open your squad’s emergency contacts on your phone.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A request to your club is sent for you
A short guide opens

lessons.film_brief: A club first-aider showing the kit and the three steps beside a pitch. No staged injuries with children.

lessons.title: Being a safe adult
lessons.one_line: In view, in the open, through the club
lessons.idea: A few plain rules protect children and protect you. Stay in view, keep messages inside the club’s channels with a parent included, and keep your check current.
steps: Never be alone and out of sight with a child.
Message players under 15 through a parent. Clean Sheet does this for you.
Photos and film only where the family has agreed.
words_to_use: Let’s talk over here where your dad can see us.
lessons.instead_of: Private messages. Lifts with one child. Changing rooms.
lessons.try_task: Check that your Working with Children Check shows as current, and read your club’s code of conduct.

answers.then: Carry on in order

answers.answer: My check has expired or isn’t recorded
answers.then: Your club’s welfare officer is told, and you get the renewal link
A reminder in three days

lessons.film_brief: Your club’s welfare officer, to camera, giving the three rules and why they protect the coach as well. Under two minutes.

lessons.title: When something worries you
lessons.one_line: You don’t investigate. You tell the right person today
lessons.idea: If a child tells you something, or you see something that doesn’t sit right, your job is to listen, write it down and pass it on the same day.
steps: Listen. Don’t promise to keep it secret.
Write down what they said, in their words.
Tell your welfare officer today. Immediate danger: call 000.
words_to_use: Thank you for telling me.
I can’t keep this to myself. I need to tell someone who can help.
lessons.instead_of: Asking lots of questions. Confronting anyone yourself.
lessons.try_task: Find your welfare officer’s name and the “Raise a concern” button, and save their number.

answers.then: Module finished. Your club is told the module is done, nothing else

answers.answer: We don’t seem to have one
answers.then: Your director is told a coach couldn’t find the welfare officer
A reminder in three days

lessons.film_brief: Your club’s welfare officer explaining what happens after a coach reports, so it feels safe to do. No case details.

modules.title: Running the session
modules.summary: Start fast, keep them busy, stop it less
modules.outcome: You can run an hour where players are busy, listening when it matters, and playing the rest of the time.

why.text: In one study of youth sessions, players spent about a third of the time standing and listening.
Coaches take up an idea when they can try it in their own sessions and see it work.

modules.leave_with: An arrival game, one attention signal, and three ways to change any game on the spot.
own_team_tiles: Players standing still, your three counts

lessons.title: Starting with a game
lessons.one_line: They play from the minute they arrive
lessons.idea: An arrival game means the first child to turn up is playing within a minute, and late arrivals just join in. Nobody waits.
steps: Pick a game that works with any number.
Start it with the first two players.
Add each arrival without stopping.
words_to_use: Jump in. You’re with the blues.
Keep going, I’ll add people.
lessons.instead_of: Standing in a circle until everyone is here.
lessons.try_task: Start the arrival game with whoever is there at 5:00, even if it is two players.

answers.then: Carry on in order
An arrival game for two is added to your library
Your poll message to families is changed to ask for 4:55

own_team_clip.example_caption: Four players passing in a circle while they wait. A game would have had them moving.

lessons.film_brief: A real session at 5:00 with two players, then five, then nine, the same game growing. Time on screen.

lessons.title: Keeping everyone busy
lessons.one_line: More balls, smaller groups, no queues
lessons.idea: If you can see a queue, split it. Two small games beat one big one, and a ball each beats one between ten.
steps: Count the balls in play. Add more.
Split any group bigger than six.
Give spare players a job: target, scorer or joker.
words_to_use: Two games now. You four over there.
Edie, you play for whoever has the ball.
lessons.instead_of: One line, one ball, one go each.
lessons.try_task: Run both middle games in two squares, not one. Use the spare player as a joker.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A tip on where to stand is added
Your sessions are proposed for one group until numbers rise

own_team_clip.example_caption: Seven players in a line waiting for a shot. Each gets one touch a minute.

lessons.film_brief: The same shooting practice two ways: one line of ten, then three small games. A touch counter on each.

lessons.title: Getting their attention without shouting
lessons.one_line: One signal, wait, then speak
lessons.idea: Shouting over noise teaches them that noise is fine. One signal, a pause until it is quiet, then a few words works better and saves your voice.
steps: Give your signal. Say nothing.
Wait until every ball is still.
Speak for 20 seconds, then restart.
words_to_use: Thank you, Leo, ball under your foot.
Eyes here. One thing.
lessons.instead_of: Talking while balls are still moving.
lessons.try_at: Each time you stop a game
lessons.try_task: Use the signal and count in your head until it is quiet before you speak. Notice how long it takes.

answers.then: Carry on in order
We suggest practising the signal as a game next week
A 30-second film on making the signal a game

lessons.film_brief: A coach raising a hand and waiting, in real time, with a counter. Then the same coach shouting, for contrast. Shot from the players’ side.

lessons.title: One game, three versions
lessons.one_line: Change the space, the numbers or a rule
lessons.idea: You don’t need more drills. You need one game and three ways to change it. Your federation’s courses teach the same idea.
steps: Too hard: bigger space or fewer defenders.
Too easy: smaller space or fewer touches.
Uneven: move one player or add a joker.
words_to_use: Same game. This time the square is smaller.
Blues get an extra player.
lessons.instead_of: Changing to a different drill every five minutes.
lessons.try_task: Play keep-ball three ways in fifteen minutes: as planned, then two touches, then a smaller square.

answers.then: Carry on in order
That version is dropped from your run sheets
We ask again next week

lessons.film_brief: One keep-ball game filmed from above, changed three times with a caption for each change. No talking head.

lessons.title: Finishing on a game
lessons.one_line: Let them play, then two minutes together
lessons.idea: The last game is theirs. Say almost nothing while it runs. Then two minutes together: one question, one thing they did well, and everyone carries something in.
steps: Start the final game on time, whatever happened before.
Stay quiet. Let them solve it.
End with one question and one thing done well.
words_to_use: What did we get better at tonight?
I saw lots of you look before the ball came. Brilliant.
lessons.instead_of: Coaching every pass of the final game.
lessons.try_task: Give yourself a limit of three comments in the whole final game.

answers.then: Carry on in order
“Your own sideline” moves up in Match day

answers.answer: Ran out of time for the game
answers.then: Your sessions are proposed with shorter middle parts

own_team_clip.example_caption: The final game. Count the instructions from the sideline in these 20 seconds.

lessons.film_brief: A final game with the coach silent on the touchline, then the two-minute huddle. Audio of the players, not the coach.

modules.title: Talking to players
modules.summary: Ask, praise and correct so it sticks
modules.outcome: You can ask, praise and correct in a few words, without stopping the game.

why.text: In one study of youth sessions, players spent about a third of the time standing and listening.
Coaches mostly ask closed questions that want a quick right answer.

modules.leave_with: Three questions, three ways to praise and one way to correct, saved to your run sheet in your own words.

lessons.title: Say less
lessons.one_line: Thirty seconds, then let them play
lessons.idea: Every minute you talk is a minute they are not playing. Say the one thing, in under thirty seconds, and get out of the way.
steps: Decide your one point before you stop the game.
Say it in two sentences.
Restart. Add the next point later.
words_to_use: One thing: look before it comes. Play.
lessons.instead_of: Three points in one stop.
lessons.try_at: Each time you stop a game
lessons.try_task: Ask your helper to time your three longest talks. Aim for under thirty seconds each.

answers.then: Carry on in order
Carry on, with a timer tip on your run sheet
This lesson repeats in three weeks

own_team_clip.example_caption: A stop that ran for just over a minute. Nine players standing.

lessons.film_brief: A coach giving the same point twice: once in 90 seconds, once in 20. A clock on screen. Players’ faces in shot.

lessons.title: Asking a question, not giving an answer
lessons.one_line: “Where is the space?” beats “pass it wide”
lessons.idea: When you tell a player the answer, they do it once. When they find it, they keep it.
steps: Let the game run for two minutes.
Ask one open question to the group.
Count to five. Take any answer. Play on.
words_to_use: Where is the space?
What did you see before it came?
Who could have helped?
What would you try next time?
lessons.instead_of: “Pass it wide.” “Spread out.” “Look up.”
lessons.try_task: After the second swap, stop both squares for 20 seconds and ask “Where is the space?” Then play on. Once is enough.

answers.then: Carry on in order
“Wait for the answer” is next
“One thing at a time” moves up, with a tip on asking one player by name
“Wait for the answer” is next

own_team_clip.example_caption: Ari has space on his left and doesn’t see it. A moment like this is where the question helps.

lessons.film_brief: Mark Dunn with U9 Mark: the same moment coached by telling, then by asking. We hear the players’ answers.

lessons.title: Wait for the answer
lessons.one_line: Count to five. Silence is thinking
lessons.idea: Silence after a question feels long to you and short to them. If you fill it, they learn to wait for you. Count to five in your head.
steps: Ask the question once.
Count to five. Don’t rephrase.
Still nothing? Ask them to tell a partner first.
words_to_use: Take your time.
Tell the person next to you, then tell me.
lessons.instead_of: Answering your own question.
lessons.try_task: Ask one question and count to five before you say anything else. Notice who speaks first.

answers.then: Carry on in order

answers.answer: I got to five and nothing
answers.then: A tip on “tell a partner” is added
This lesson repeats next week

lessons.film_brief: One question asked, then five full seconds of silence on screen before a child answers. The counter is the film.

lessons.title: Praise the effort, name the action
lessons.one_line: “Great first touch away from him” beats “well done”
lessons.idea: “Well done” tells a child you’re pleased. Naming what they did tells them what to do again. Praise the try as much as the result.
steps: Catch them doing the thing you are working on.
Say their name and name the action.
Praise the attempt even when it didn’t come off.
words_to_use: Jun, great look over your shoulder.
Good idea, Poppy. Wrong pass, right idea.
I love that you tried it.
lessons.instead_of: “Well done.” “Unlucky.” Praise only for goals.
lessons.try_task: Give every player one piece of named praise. Tick them off on your run sheet as you go.

answers.then: Carry on in order
The players you missed are shown first next week
A reminder is pinned to the top of your run sheet

own_team_clip.example_caption: Poppy tries to turn her defender and loses it. This is the try to praise.

lessons.film_brief: A run of named praise from a real coach, each matched to the action it praises in slow motion.

lessons.title: Fixing a mistake without stopping the game
lessons.one_line: A word to one player while the rest play on
lessons.idea: Most mistakes need one player to hear one thing. Stopping everyone for it costs eight others their game. Walk alongside and say it quietly.
steps: Let the mistake go once. Is it a pattern?
Step in next to the player as play goes on.
One question or one cue. Step away.
words_to_use: Next time, where could your first touch go?
Try opening your body. Go again.
lessons.instead_of: Freezing the game to show everyone what one player did wrong.
lessons.try_task: Correct two players this way without stopping the game at all.

answers.then: Carry on in order
Carry on in order
“Say less” repeats, with your stop count from the run sheet

lessons.film_brief: A coach walking beside a player mid-game, lapel microphone on, six seconds of talk, game never stops.

lessons.title: One thing at a time
lessons.one_line: One focus per game, even when you see five
lessons.idea: You will always see five things to fix. Players can hold one. Pick the one your session is built on and let the rest go until next week.
steps: Write tonight’s one thing at the top of your run sheet.
Praise and correct only that.
Note the others for next week’s session.
words_to_use: Tonight is all about your first touch.
lessons.instead_of: A different coaching point every minute.
lessons.try_task: Coach only the session’s main idea. Put everything else you notice into your three taps afterwards.

answers.then: Module finished
Carry on, with the one thing pinned on your run sheet
This lesson repeats in a fortnight

lessons.film_brief: The same two minutes of a game twice: once with five different instructions shouted, once with one. Players’ reactions.

modules.title: Match day
modules.summary: Team talk, fair turns, your own sideline
modules.outcome: You can run a match day that is calm, fair to every player, and ties back to training.

why.text: Children whose coaches were trained to encourage effort were far more likely to come back the next season.
Your club’s fair-turns rule applies to every team at this age.

modules.leave_with: A one-minute team talk, a turns plan made before you leave home, and a rule for your own voice.
own_team_tiles: Minutes on the pitch, most and least
Players who have tried in goal

lessons.title: The team talk in one minute
lessons.one_line: One idea, from Tuesday
lessons.idea: Before a game, players can hold one idea. Make it the thing you worked on at training, and say it in a sentence they could repeat.
steps: Say who starts where. Clean Sheet has it ready.
Give the one idea from training.
Finish with something about enjoying it.
words_to_use: Today, see if you can look before the ball comes.
Try things. Mistakes are fine.
lessons.instead_of: Tactics on a whiteboard. Talk about the other team.
lessons.try_task: Give your team talk in under a minute. Ask one player to say the one idea back to you.

answers.answer: Under a minute, and they knew it
answers.then: Carry on in order
“Say less” is added to your Sunday reminders
Tuesday’s idea is shown on your match-day screen

lessons.film_brief: A real pre-game huddle, 50 seconds, uncut. Then one player repeating the idea to camera.

lessons.title: Fair turns
lessons.one_line: Decide before you leave home
lessons.idea: Fair playing time is easy to believe in and hard to do in the moment. Decide the changes before the game and let the plan make the calls.
steps: Open Sunday’s turns. They are lined up for you.
Check who has played least and who hasn’t been in goal.
Follow the plan, whatever the score.
words_to_use: Mack, you’re on at the next break.
Everyone plays the same today.
lessons.instead_of: Leaving your strongest players on because it’s close.
lessons.try_task: Open the turns plan, make any swaps, and follow it for the whole game.

answers.then: Carry on in order
We show what the change did to minutes, and ask why
A two-minute film on reading the turns plan

lessons.film_brief: A coach at the kitchen table on Friday night setting the turns in two minutes, then the bench on Sunday running to plan.

lessons.title: Your own sideline
lessons.one_line: Let them play. Say less than you want to
lessons.idea: During a game, instructions arrive too late to help and take the decision away from the player. Encourage, and save the coaching for the breaks.
steps: Stand still, near halfway.
Praise effort and good ideas by name.
Keep instructions for half-time.
words_to_use: Great idea, Sol.
Unlucky. Try it again.
lessons.instead_of: “Pass!” “Shoot!” “Man on!” Telling the player on the ball what to do.
lessons.try_task: Give no instructions to the player on the ball in the first half. Praise only.

answers.then: Carry on in order
Carry on in order
We suggest asking your assistant to tap your arm each time

own_team_clip.example_caption: Listen to the touchline in this minute. Count the instructions.

lessons.film_brief: Match footage with sideline audio isolated: first with constant instruction, then with praise only. Same team.

lessons.title: Half-time in three minutes
lessons.one_line: Drink, one question, one thing
lessons.idea: Half-time is short and they are tired. A drink, one question to them, one thing from you, and back out.
steps: Drinks first. Say nothing for a minute.
Ask: what is working?
Give the one idea again, and the changes.
words_to_use: What’s working out there?
Second half, same idea: look before it comes.
lessons.instead_of: A list of everything that went wrong.
lessons.try_task: Ask “what’s working?” before you say anything about the game.

answers.then: Carry on in order
“Wait for the answer” is offered again
“Say less” is added to your Sunday reminders

lessons.film_brief: A real half-time, three minutes, uncut, with a clock in the corner.

lessons.title: After the whistle
lessons.one_line: Win or lose, the same three things
lessons.idea: What you do in the five minutes after a game teaches them what mattered. Make it the same every week, whatever the result.
steps: Shake hands with the other team and the referee.
Name one thing the team did that came from training.
Do your three taps before you drive home.
words_to_use: Thank you, ref.
I saw so many of you look before the ball came.
lessons.instead_of: The score. The referee. What went wrong.
lessons.try_task: Name one thing from training that you saw, then do your three taps in the car park.

answers.then: Module finished. Tuesday’s session is built from your taps
A reminder at 6 pm
A short film on talking to a team after a heavy loss

lessons.film_brief: The five minutes after a loss, handled well. Handshakes, one sentence, players leaving smiling.

modules.title: Parents and your helpers
modules.summary: Set it up once so the season runs
modules.outcome: You have told parents what to expect, shared the jobs, and know how to handle a hard conversation.

why.text: Coaches take up an idea when they can try it in their own setting and see it work.
Your club’s rules on who can message whom apply to everything here.

modules.leave_with: A welcome message in your words, a jobs list with names on it, and a way to answer a complaint.
own_team_tiles: Families who have read your welcome

lessons.title: Your first message to parents
lessons.one_line: What to expect from you this season
lessons.idea: Most trouble with parents comes from surprise. Tell them at the start how you coach, how turns work and how to reach you.
steps: Open the draft Clean Sheet has written for you.
Change it into your own words.
Send it before the first game.
words_to_use: Everyone gets fair time, in every position.
I’ll ask questions more than I give answers.
The best way to reach me is a message here.
lessons.instead_of: Saying nothing and hoping it goes well.
lessons.try_task: Edit the welcome draft and send it to your families.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A reminder in two days
A reminder before your next game

lessons.film_brief: A coach reading their own welcome message aloud, over shots of the season starting. Under 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The parents’ sideline
lessons.one_line: Ask them to cheer, not to coach
lessons.idea: Players can’t listen to you and a parent at once. Ask parents early, and kindly, to cheer for effort and leave the coaching to training.
steps: Ask once, to everyone, in your welcome.
Thank parents who do it well.
If one keeps coaching, have a quiet word, or ask your manager to.
words_to_use: Could you help me? Cheer everything, coach nothing.
They hear you more than me. That’s why I’m asking.
lessons.instead_of: Calling a parent out in front of the team.
lessons.try_task: Thank the parents as a group for cheering, before the game starts.

answers.then: Carry on in order
A short script for a quiet word, and your manager’s number
Your club’s welfare officer is suggested. You choose whether to contact them

lessons.film_brief: A team manager talking about the one conversation that changed their sideline. No footage of real parents behaving badly.

lessons.title: Sharing the load
lessons.one_line: Ask for one small job each
lessons.idea: People say yes to a small, named job and no to “can anyone help?”. Five jobs, five names, and you can coach.
steps: Open the jobs list for your team.
Ask one person for one job, by name.
Thank them in front of the group.
words_to_use: Kerem, could you be game leader this Sunday? It’s 50 minutes.
Thanks, Dana, for the kit this week.
lessons.instead_of: Doing it all yourself. A general call for volunteers.
lessons.try_task: Fill the one job that is still open by asking one person directly.

answers.then: Carry on in order
Two more names are suggested from who comes most often
A reminder on Thursday

lessons.film_brief: A coach asking one parent for one job at pick-up. Fifteen seconds. Then the same pitch on Sunday with five people helping.

lessons.title: A hard conversation
lessons.one_line: Listen first, use the record, offer a time
lessons.idea: When a parent is unhappy, usually about game time or position, they want to be heard. Listen, show what the record says, and offer a proper time to talk.
steps: Not on the sideline. Offer a catch-up.
Listen all the way through before you answer.
Show the turns record. Say what you will do next.
words_to_use: I can hear this matters. Can we talk properly on Tuesday at 4:45?
Here are the minutes for the last five games.
Here’s what I’ll do.
lessons.instead_of: Defending yourself on the spot. Promising a position.
lessons.try_task: Find where to offer a catch-up time and where the turns record is, so you are ready.

answers.then: Course finished. Your season page shows what you have tried

answers.answer: I have one of these now
answers.then: A catch-up is drafted, and your mentor is suggested
No reminder. It’s here when you need it

lessons.film_brief: Two coaches role-playing the conversation both ways: defensive, then listening. No real families.
